title: Inside Long Context: Cached Keys, Evicted Tokens and Scattered Evidence
dek: A long prompt becomes a cache that grows with every token. We follow one contract question through prefill, decoding and eviction, to the place where length stops being the hard part.
by: Draft for team review · written by Claude Code from published research and engineering writing · checked in code
lead: What is a context window? It's the span of tokens a model can attend to at once, stored as a KV cache that grows with every token. Length costs memory. Scattered evidence costs accuracy.

cover.alt: A question node arcs down to three glowing tokens spread far apart along a long strip of dim tokens.
cover.caption: One question has to reach evidence scattered across the whole window.

description: What is a context window? Follow one long prompt through the KV cache, eviction and scattered evidence, and see where long context really breaks.
decisions: Budget KV cache memory per request before raising a context limit.
Tag test questions by evidence dispersion as well as prompt length.
Test an eviction policy on dispersed-evidence questions before trusting it.
Pre-organise material into a workspace when the same sources face repeated queries.

items.how: Copy the calculator from this post and fill in layers, KV heads and head width from an open-weight model's config file. Raise the token count step by step.
items.look_for: Memory rises in a straight line with tokens, and the bytes per token never change.

items.how: Build a long synthetic contract from filler clauses. Put a renewal clause near the start and an override for it near the end, then ask a question that needs both.
items.look_for: A correct answer cites both clauses. A half-read answer cites only the first.

items.how: Keep the same filler and length, but place the two clauses side by side. Ask the same question several times with each layout on a small local model.
items.look_for: The side-by-side layout should be answered correctly more often, matching the local-evidence result.

items.how: Run the toy eviction snippet, then move the clue's position and shrink the budget.
items.look_for: A token that early queries ignored gets dropped, even though the later question needs it.

items.how: With an eviction library of your choice, run both contract layouts at a full cache and then at smaller budgets. Record accuracy for each.
items.look_for: If the scattered layout falls first as the budget tightens, you have measured the gap in the closing section.

body.text: The window is a cache with a hard ceiling

body: You paste a long supplier contract into a chat and ask one question. Does the renewal clause near the front survive the termination rules buried in the appendix? The model answers confidently, citing only the front. Nothing crashed. The appendix sat in the window the whole time, and the answer never touched it. We'll follow that one question through the machinery, stage by stage.

So what is a context window? It's the longest run of tokens a model can condition on in one pass. Tokens are the sub-word pieces a tokenizer cuts text into. Everything inside the window can, in principle, shape every next token. Everything outside it doesn't exist. The catch hides in that phrase, in principle. Being present and being used are separate events.

Evaluations, as the LURCH authors put it, «typically treat context length as the main indicator of difficulty». We think that framing hides two separate bills. One is memory and compute, paid per token you add. The other is reasoning, paid per piece of evidence you scatter. Our contract question pays both. Let's open the first bill.

body.text: Prefill writes a key and a value for every token

body: Here's what happens when you hit send. The model runs prefill, one pass over the whole prompt. At every layer, each token is projected into a query, a key and a value. Attention scores a token's query against earlier keys and blends their values. The keys and values are kept. That stored stack is the KV cache. It's why generation never recomputes the prompt.

The size is plain arithmetic. Per token, you store one key and one value per layer, per KV head, each `head_dim` numbers wide. So `cache_bytes = tokens × layers × kv_heads × head_dim × (K and V) × bytes_per_number`. Every factor but tokens is fixed by the architecture. Tokens is the one you control. The DropKV authors name the result: a bottleneck in «long-context scenarios due to linear memory growth».

Linear sounds gentle. It isn't, because the cache lives in accelerator memory beside the weights. A long contract claims a big share of that memory, and every concurrent request brings its own copy. Fewer requests fit in a batch, so each answer costs more. Run the calculator below with your own model card's numbers. The ceiling stops being abstract fast.

body.label: KV cache size per request (illustrative config, plug in your own)
body.source:
def kv_cache_bytes(tokens, layers, kv_heads, head_dim, bytes_per_number=2):
    # one key and one value per token, per layer, per KV head
    per_token = layers * kv_heads * head_dim * 2 * bytes_per_number
    return tokens * per_token

cfg = dict(layers=32, kv_heads=8, head_dim=128)  # a hypothetical model
for tokens in (8_000, 32_000, 128_000):
    gb = kv_cache_bytes(tokens, **cfg) / 1e9
    print(f"{tokens:>7} tokens -> {gb:5.1f} GB per request")

body.text: Decoding rereads the whole cache for each new token

body: Prefill is done. Now the model writes its answer one token at a time. Each new token produces a fresh query, and that query is scored against every cached key. A softmax turns the scores into weights that sum to one. The output is a weighted blend of cached values. Then the new token's own key and value join the cache.

Two costs fall out of that loop. Decoding is memory-bound: every step reads the full cache, so a longer prompt slows each generated token. Prefill is compute-bound, because every token attends to every earlier one. That work grows faster than the prompt does. Short answers over long prompts spend most of their time in prefill. Long answers spend it streaming the cache.

Then there's the quiet failure. Softmax has one unit of weight to share across every key. Add many tokens that look vaguely relevant, and each real clue gets a thinner slice. Our appendix clause competes with every other clause that mentions renewal. Nothing in the arithmetic says it wins. That's the mechanism behind a confident, half-read answer.

body.text: Eviction decides which cached tokens to forget

body: If the cache is too big, drop some of it. That's KV cache eviction: score each cached token, keep the best ones within a budget, discard the rest. Early methods scored by attention alone, keeping keys that past queries looked at most. The risk is obvious. A clue ignored early can become essential later. Our appendix clause fits that profile exactly.

body.alt: A full token cache is scored and trimmed; the appendix clue is evicted and a later query points at its empty slot.
body.caption: Attention-based eviction keeps what early queries read, so a clue needed later can vanish.

body: We went through the DropKV abstract to see how its authors frame the scoring problem. The ideal is to drop whichever set of tokens disturbs the output least. They call that joint choice «an NP-hard combinatorial problem». Their move is to split it, «decoupling the joint eviction decision into independent per-token scoring». Per-token scores can be sorted and cut. That's cheap, and it suits a GPU kernel.

The payoff is speed plus a guarantee. Their kernels skip building the full attention matrix, and the abstract reports «up to a 9.9% matched-batch end-to-end prefill speedup». It also claims a «provable constant-factor approximation guarantee under a cone condition». We like that the guarantee names its assumption out loud. We'd still want to know how often real prompts break it.

body.label: Toy attention-score eviction that drops a late-needed clue (illustrative)
body.source:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n, budget = 1000, 200
past_attention = rng.random(n) * 0.1   # how much early queries read each token
past_attention[:50] += 0.5             # the opening clauses everyone read
appendix_clue = 900                    # needed only by a later question

keep = np.argsort(past_attention)[-budget:]
print("appendix clue kept?", appendix_clue in keep)

body.text: Scattered evidence is the difficulty length hides

body: Now the surprising part. A new arXiv paper on long-context reasoning argues that length is the wrong dial. «Contexts of equal length can pose very different challenges», its authors write. One question is answerable from a single local passage. Another needs clues spread across the whole window. Same token count, same cache, same bill. Very different odds.

body.alt: Two bars of equal length: clustered clues reach the answer in one hop, spread clues need a chain of hops.
body.caption: Same length and same cache, yet dispersed evidence demands a longer chain of dependent steps.

body: The LURCH authors split difficulty into three properties. Evidence scope is how much necessary information must be found. Evidence dispersion is how widely it's scattered. Reasoning depth counts the dependent steps from evidence to answer. Their benchmark of 6,550 instances ships with «supporting evidence and reasoning graphs», so each property can be measured per question.

The results map onto our contract question. At fixed length, all three properties are «strongly negatively correlated with model performance». As length grows, accuracy «degrades sharply on samples with dispersed evidence», yet holds up when evidence is local. And difficulty compounds: moderate values on all three are harder than one extreme value. Our renewal question is moderate everywhere. That's the worst spot.

body.text: Curation moves the reading before the question

body: If scattered evidence is the hard case, one fix is to stop scattering it. The Librarian Agents paper does that ahead of time. A builder agent turns raw documents into «a hierarchical filesystem of synthetic files and reference links». A separate answering agent then works inside that workspace. The renewal clause and its appendix override could share one folder, cross-linked.

The training signal is the clever bit. Workspace construction is framed as a Markov decision process, a sequence of actions with a reward at the end. The builder is trained «via reinforcement learning to directly maximize downstream answering accuracy». So it learns what a future reader will need. Against the strongest retrieval and precomputation baselines, it wins «by 33 percentage points on BrowseComp-Plus».

A survey of memory-centric compression supplies the vocabulary. It separates «compute-active memory, which directly participates in model computation» from memory stored outside the computation path. The window is compute-active, so you pay for every token in it. A curated workspace costs nothing until it's injected. In our view the survey names the real problem: «deciding which information should participate in costly inference, when, and in what form».

body.text: Dispersion under an eviction budget is uncharted

body: Here's the gap that bugs us. Eviction methods get scored on suites like RULER and LongBench at fixed cache budgets. LURCH scores reasoning difficulty with a full context, as far as its abstract says. Neither line of work, as described, crosses the two. Does a per-token scorer drop dispersed clues faster than local ones? We suspect it does. Nobody has shown it.

The suspicion is mechanical. A scorer judges a token by its effect on the outputs computed so far. A dispersed clue matters only when a later step needs it, and the early steps may not. Reasoning depth makes that worse, since late steps lean on early ones. So the evicted token and the failed answer can sit far apart in time.

You can probe this on a laptop. Take questions tagged by dispersion and run them with a full cache, then at shrinking budgets. Plot accuracy against budget, one line for local evidence and one for dispersed. If the lines part as the budget tightens, eviction is spending your accuracy on exactly the hard questions. The lab below sets it up.
What is a context window in an LLM?

A context window is the longest run of tokens a model can attend to in one pass. Everything inside it can shape the next token, and anything outside is invisible. Inside the model, the window lives as a KV cache that grows with every token. A bigger window therefore costs memory as well as compute, and a busy server feels both.
Does a bigger context window mean better long context answers?

Not by itself. A longer window lets more text in, but it doesn't make scattered clues easier to combine. The LURCH authors found that as length grows, accuracy «degrades sharply on samples with dispersed evidence», and stays relatively stable when evidence is local. Where your evidence sits matters as much as how much fits.

KV cache eviction drops some cached keys and values so a long prompt fits a memory budget. A scorer ranks cached tokens and keeps the best ones. Older methods ranked by attention alone. DropKV splits the choice «into independent per-token scoring» and reports that it «consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines at equivalent cache budgets» on RULER and LongBench.
